title: Recognizable separability of automatic relations
formal: Is the following recognizable-separability problem undecidable, as asserted by Conjecture 7.1 of the source? Given a finite alphabet \(A\) and two nondeterministic finite automata representing binary automatic relations \(R_1,R_2\subseteq A^*\times A^*\), decide whether there exist \(k\in\mathbb N\) and regular languages \(L_1,\ldots,L_k,K_1,\ldots,K_k\subseteq A^*\) with \[R_1\subseteq S,\qquad S\cap R_2=\varnothing,\qquad S=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}(L_i\times K_i).\] The number \(k\) and the sizes of all component automata have no prescribed finite bound. Undecidability means that no deterministic Turing machine halts and gives the correct answer on every finite input description of this kind.

source_formulation.text: The Rec-separability problem – or, equivalently, the regular colorability problem – is undecidable.
source_formulation.caption: Conjecture 7.1, source statement; MFCS 2023, p. 17:13

why: Automatic relations allow a finite machine to compare positions in two unbounded strings. Recognizable relations replace this synchronization with finitely many independent regular tests. Deciding whether such a replacement can separate two specifications is a basic abstraction question connected to regular colorings of infinite graphs and to simplifying relational constraints. Its answer would locate an effective boundary between two elementary finite descriptions of infinite relations.
status_note: Source-open: the MFCS 2023 statement is Conjecture 7.1, not a theorem. Morvan’s 22 May 2025 thesis retains the unrestricted question as Open Problem VII.1.10. The February 2026 automatic-structure dichotomy concerns a fixed finite target and does not resolve the existentially unbounded separator size. Checked on 15 September 2026 with a bounded later-work search; no cited proof was independently formalized.

progress.text: Theorem 3.1 gives polynomial-time reductions in both directions between binary recognizable separation and finite regular colorability of automatic graphs. Theorems 4.4 and 5.6 prove undecidability for each fixed color or product bound of at least two; Conjecture 7.1 proposes undecidability for unrestricted separation.
Morvan’s thesis, Open Problem VII.1.10 and Chapter X.1, explicitly says the unrestricted recognizable-separability problem remains open.

Cuvelier and Morvan’s preprint gives a decidability dichotomy for homomorphisms from automatic structures to a fixed finite target, including the regular-homomorphism variant. Fixing that target fixes the palette in coloring instances; the result does not decide whether some finite palette exists.

The conjecture, complete binary-relation definitions, and later thesis and preprint scopes were checked. A bounded search found no resolution of the unrestricted target; the source conjecture is not presented as an established undecidability theorem.

importance.reason: This is the unrestricted separation problem between two fundamental classes of word relations. Its equivalence to finite regular colorability links finite-state abstraction, automatic structures and relational constraints, while known fixed-bound undecidability leaves the central unbounded formulation unresolved.
importance.basis: Individual assessment from the MFCS 2023 formulation and reductions and Morvan’s 2025 thesis discussion.

sentences: Binary automatic relations are recognized by finite automata reading padded pairs of words synchronously.
The question asks whether it is undecidable to separate two such relations by a finite union of products of regular languages.
The number of products is existentially chosen with no prescribed upper bound.
Fixed-bound separation is already undecidable, but the unrestricted problem remains explicitly open in the checked later thesis.
A resolution would clarify when synchronized infinite relations admit effective separation by finitely many independent regular tests.

definitions: For \(u,v\in A^*\), their convolution \(u\otimes v\) has length \(\max\{|u|,|v|\}\). Its \(j\)-th symbol is the pair of \(j\)-th letters, using a fresh padding symbol \(\bot\notin A\) when \(j\) exceeds one word's length. Padding occurs only at the end of the shorter component; \(\varepsilon\otimes\varepsilon=\varepsilon\). An input automaton \(B\) over \((A\cup\{\bot\})^2\) represents \(R(B)=\{(u,v):B\text{ accepts }u\otimes v\}\). Only valid convolutions affect this relation. A nondeterministic finite automaton has a finite state set, designated initial and accepting state sets, and a finite letter-labeled transition relation; it accepts a finite word if some path with that label leads from an initial state to an accepting state. A language is regular if some such automaton accepts it. A recognizable binary relation is a finite union of Cartesian products of two regular languages, as displayed above; \(k=0\) gives the empty relation. All alphabets, state sets and transition lists are explicit finite input data, with symbol and state indices encoded as binary integers with delimiters. Both relations are binary, as in the source's main formulation; neither has to be symmetric. There is no promise that they are disjoint. The quantifier over candidate separators is inside the decision problem and ranges over all finite descriptions; it is not a fixed bound supplied to the deciding machine. One uniform machine would have to decide every instance, using finite computation and no advice or oracle. No complexity bound is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the defined input language is undecidable, or refute the conjecture by supplying a uniform total decision algorithm and proving its correctness and termination in Lean. A proof of undecidability must exclude every total computable decider for unrestricted finite recognizable separators. Undecidability when the number of Cartesian products is fixed, or when the input relations are asynchronous rational relations, does not prove this conjecture.

context_blocks.text: A synchronous automaton can inspect matching positions in the two component words. In one Cartesian product, by contrast, the first component is checked independently of the second. Taking finitely many such products allows finitely many alternatives, while retaining independent tests within each alternative.

Separation permits an overapproximation: the separator may contain pairs outside both input relations. This differs from asking whether one automatic relation is itself recognizable, which is already decidable. The difference is the freedom to choose what happens on pairs not constrained by either input.

The source connects unrestricted recognizable separation to coloring an automatic graph with finitely many colors, each color class a regular language. An automatic graph has words as vertices and a synchronously recognized edge relation; adjacent vertices must receive different colors. The number of colors is existentially chosen and unbounded.

The published fixed-product-count and fixed-color-count undecidability results do not settle the unrestricted question. A pair with no separator of one prescribed size may have a larger separator. Morvan’s later thesis continues to identify this unbounded version as an open problem.
